body:
The disciples are hungry. They pick heads of grain, rub them between their fingers, and eat. It is such a small detail that we might wonder why Luke even mentions it. But that movement of their hands is exactly what the Pharisees notice. To them, rubbing the grain could be considered work on the Sabbath.

And suddenly I wonder how often we do the same thing.

They were watching the disciples’ fingers while God Himself was walking beside them.

The Pharisees were not wrong to care about the Sabbath. It was sacred. Their mistake was allowing their understanding of the law to become so consuming that they could no longer recognize the One the law was pointing toward.

Jesus reminds them of David eating the sacred bread when he and his companions were hungry. Then He says something astonishing: “The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.”

Perhaps one of the greatest dangers in our spiritual lives is not always doing something obviously wrong. Sometimes it is becoming so certain that we are right that we stop looking for God.

We can know Scripture and still miss its heart. We can defend our beliefs and forget compassion. We can notice another person’s smallest failure while remaining completely unaware of what God may be doing in that person’s life. We can become so occupied with the grain between someone’s fingers that we fail to see Christ standing beside them.

And perhaps this Gospel asks an uncomfortable question:

What am I watching so closely that I might be missing Jesus?

The rules mattered. The Sabbath mattered. But mercy mattered too. The Pharisees saw a violation. Jesus saw hungry men.

Maybe faith requires more than knowing what is right. It requires a heart close enough to God to understand why it is right.
prayer: Lord, protect me from a faith that sees everything except You. When I become quick to judge, slow me down. When I am convinced that I am right, keep my heart humble. Give me eyes that notice the person before the fault, mercy before judgment, and above all, Your presence in the ordinary moments I so easily overlook. Amen.
title: When Being Right Makes Us Blind
